paragraphs.title: A Faithful Heart, Not External Worship

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool.”
easy.q: What does the Lord say is His throne?

answers: The poor and contrite in spirit
easy.explanation: The Lord looks to “him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word.”
easy.q: At whom will the Lord look?

easy.explanation: Isaiah says, “Yea, they have chosen their own ways.”

answers: Someone who responds to God’s word with reverence
medium.explanation: The phrase describes a person who takes the word of the Lord seriously and reverently.
medium.q: What does “trembleth at my word” describe?

answers: The people cannot find a place to sacrifice
The worshipers continue in evil and delight in abominations
Jerusalem has not yet been restored
medium.explanation: Their outward acts are condemned because their hearts and conduct remain evil.
medium.q: Why are the outward sacrifices unacceptable in verse 3?

answers: God values a humble, obedient spirit rather than empty ritual
medium.explanation: The passage contrasts humble obedience with worship that is accompanied by evil conduct.
medium.q: What is the main contrast between verses 1–2 and verse 3?

answers: To show that external worship is corrupted by sinful behavior
To describe the proper order of sacrifices
To explain how the temple was built
challenge.explanation: The comparisons show that ritual has no value when the worshiper chooses evil.
challenge.q: Why are several shocking comparisons made between sacrifices and violent or idolatrous acts?

answers: The people listened carefully to God
They did not answer or hear when God called and spoke
challenge.explanation: God says, “When I called, none did answer; when I spake, they did not hear.”
challenge.q: What caused the judgment described in verse 4?

answers: God is impressed by buildings and ceremonies above all else
God rejects every form of worship
God honors those who are humble before His word and rejects hypocritical worship
challenge.explanation: The passage teaches that true worship requires humility and obedience, not merely outward acts.

easy.explanation: The verse says, “A voice of noise from the city, a voice from the temple.”
easy.q: From where does the voice in verse 6 come?

easy.explanation: The voice is identified as “a voice of the Lord that rendereth recompence to his enemies.”
easy.q: Who renders recompence to the Lord’s enemies?

easy.explanation: Verse 8 says, “as soon as Zion travailed, she brought forth her children.”

answers: She gives birth before the pain comes
She gives birth only after many years of suffering
medium.explanation: Zion brings forth “before her pain came” and before she travailed.
medium.q: What is unusual about Zion’s birth in verse 7?

medium.explanation: The word refers to labor pains associated with childbirth.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “travailed” refer to?

answers: Judgment and redemption are presented together
Both passages discuss only temple construction
Both passages describe only priestly duties
medium.explanation: Verse 6 describes judgment, while verses 7–9 describe Zion’s sudden restoration.

answers: The remarkable speed and greatness of the change
challenge.explanation: The question highlights the sudden and extraordinary birth of a nation.
challenge.q: What does the question, “Shall the earth be made to bring forth in one day?” emphasize?

answers: To begin the process but leave it unfinished
To complete what He has begun
challenge.explanation: The Lord asks whether He would bring to the birth without causing the child to be brought forth.
challenge.q: What does the Lord promise in verse 9?

answers: Redemption is pictured as Zion quickly bringing forth her children under God’s power
Redemption is pictured only as destruction
Redemption is pictured as a process with no result
challenge.explanation: Zion’s children are born suddenly, and God guarantees that the process will be completed.
challenge.q: How does the image of birth communicate redemption?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “all ye that love her” should rejoice with Jerusalem.
easy.q: Who is told to rejoice with Jerusalem?

answers: As a nourishing and comforting mother
easy.explanation: Jerusalem is pictured as providing nourishment, satisfaction, and comfort.
easy.q: How is Jerusalem pictured in verses 11–12?

answers: As a king leading an army
As a mother comforting her child
As a judge condemning the wicked
easy.explanation: The Lord says, “As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you.”
easy.q: How does the Lord say He will comfort His people?

medium.explanation: The Lord extends peace like a river and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream.
medium.q: What do the river and flowing stream represent in verse 12?

answers: The nourishing abundance of her comfort
medium.explanation: The image continues the picture of Jerusalem as a mother nourishing her children.
medium.q: What does the phrase “the breasts of her consolations” suggest?

answers: Joy for the Lord’s servants and indignation toward His enemies
The joy of slaves and the sadness of kings
The peace of the Gentiles and the building of the temple
medium.explanation: The verse reveals the Lord’s hand toward His servants and His indignation toward His enemies.

answers: From a comforting mother to a source of peace, glory, and consolation
From a warring city to a ruined city
From a place of judgment to an empty land
challenge.explanation: Jerusalem is first pictured as a mother and then as the source of abundant peace and comfort.
challenge.q: How does the picture of Jerusalem develop through verses 10–13?

answers: It is personal, tender, and secure
It is offered only to enemies
challenge.explanation: The comparison to a mother emphasizes intimate and protective comfort.
challenge.q: What does the motherly image teach about the Lord’s consolation?

answers: The abundance brings satisfaction, delight, and rejoicing
The abundance causes the people to leave Jerusalem
The abundance is only a punishment for enemies
challenge.explanation: The people will be satisfied, delighted, comforted, and joyful because of Jerusalem’s abundance.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between Jerusalem’s abundance and the people’s joy?

paragraphs.title: The Fire of Judgment and the Mission to the Nations

answers: Fire and chariots like a whirlwind
easy.explanation: The Lord comes with fire and chariots like a whirlwind.
easy.q: With what does the Lord come to judgment?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I will gather all nations and tongues.”
The nations bring the brethren to “my holy mountain Jerusalem.”
easy.q: Where do the nations bring the Lord’s people?

answers: To judge all flesh and punish the wicked
medium.explanation: The Lord pleads with all flesh by fire and sword, and many are slain.
medium.q: What is the purpose of the fire and sword in verses 15–16?

answers: A survivor or one who has escaped judgment
medium.explanation: Those who escape are survivors whom the Lord sends to the nations.
medium.q: What is an “escape” in verse 19 best understood to mean?

answers: To declare the Lord’s glory to distant peoples
medium.explanation: They are sent to nations that have not heard of the Lord’s fame or seen His glory.
medium.q: What is the task of those who escape and are sent to the nations?

answers: The passage moves from judgment by fire to mission and the gathering of nations
The passage moves from comfort to temple construction
The passage moves from worship to the end of pilgrimage
challenge.explanation: After describing judgment, the passage describes messengers going to the nations and the return of the brethren.
challenge.q: What major movement occurs in verses 15–21?

answers: The nations participate in bringing the scattered people to Jerusalem
The nations remain entirely separated from Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The nations are pictured as helping bring the Lord’s people to His holy mountain.
challenge.q: What does the nations’ act of bringing the brethren as an offering imply?

answers: Only the original Israelites may return
Some of those gathered will serve in worship
The priests and Levites will be replaced only by Gentiles
challenge.explanation: The Lord says, “I will also take of them for priests and for Levites.”
challenge.q: What does the Lord’s choosing priests and Levites from among them suggest?

paragraphs.title: A Renewed World, Universal Worship, and the Shame of the Wicked

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “so shall your seed and your name remain.”
easy.q: What will remain before the Lord like the new heavens and the new earth?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “shall all flesh come to worship before me.”
easy.q: Who will come to worship before the Lord?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “their worm shall not die.”
easy.q: What will not happen to the worm of the transgressors?

answers: From one new moon to another and from one sabbath to another
medium.explanation: The passage describes worship from one new moon to another and from one sabbath to another.
medium.q: How often will all flesh come to worship before the Lord?

answers: A disgrace or object of loathing
medium.explanation: The transgressors’ corpses will be a disgrace and an object of abhorrence to all flesh.
medium.q: What does “an abhorring” mean in verse 24?

answers: Universal worship before the Lord versus the shame of the transgressors
The joy of Jerusalem versus temple construction
The return of Israel versus the sending of messengers
medium.explanation: Verse 23 describes all flesh worshiping, while verse 24 describes the lasting disgrace of the rebels.
medium.q: What contrast appears between verses 23 and 24?

answers: Both describe lasting existence before the Lord
The new heavens remove Israel’s seed
challenge.explanation: The verse compares the permanence of the new heavens and earth with the enduring seed and name of Israel.
challenge.q: How are the new heavens and new earth related to Israel’s seed and name?

answers: Worship will be widespread and continual
Only a small group will worship
Worship will end after the return
challenge.explanation: The regular repetition and reference to “all flesh” emphasize universal and ongoing worship.
challenge.q: What does the repeated worship from month to month and sabbath to sabbath emphasize?

answers: To emphasize the contrast between worship before the Lord and lasting shame
To show that worship is unimportant
To show that the transgressors become priests
challenge.explanation: The ending contrasts those who worship the Lord with those whose rebellion ends in enduring disgrace.
challenge.q: Why does the chapter end by placing the worshipers and the transgressors side by side?
